Most of the ideas come from my memory, since I really love history and most Indonesians also enjoy solving puzzles (e.g., English crossword puzzles):

My team and I mostly discuss things online. Even though my team members are busy, we keep each other updated on the progress and what needs to be finalized or improved.

Finding suitable references because most online books are paid; even when searching for references on the internet, most of the data lacks clear sources, which I fear could lead to serious errors.

Reading history, learning something new, and also when creating riddles on topics like everyday life and the kids’ world—it mostly makes me feel nostalgic and laugh

Perhaps I would expand the team to include more members and diversify the topics.

column2: I am confident that my riddles accurately reflect my national-linguistic community because they include important elements of Brazilian culture and the Portuguese language spoken in Brazil. The riddles refer to topics such as traditional dances, typical cuisine, geography, music, and important Brazilian figures, which are all connected to the country’s identity. They also show cultural knowledge that would be familiar to many Brazilians, such as regional diversity, popular traditions, and national symbols. However, I also recognize that Brazil is a very large and diverse country, so no set of riddles can represent every region, or cultural experience perfectly. Overall, I would say I am highly confident that the riddles reflect Brazilian national-linguistic culture, while still understanding that they represent only part of Brazil’s rich and diverse identity.

column19: Our selection of wildcard topics was primarily driven by the reference answers themselves. Rather than starting with a rigid category, we brainstormed culturally recognizable answers such as local fruits, everyday objects, or human anatomy that naturally fit themselves to the traditional riddle format. column22:
Idea Generation: I primarily drew from childhood memories of traditional Bengali riddles . For the wildcard topics, I often reverse-engineered the riddles and choosing a culturally significant answer first (like jackfruit or a rickshaw) .

Research & Refinement: While the traditional items came from memory, I used internet searches to rigorously fact check dates for the historical topics. I also used an AI assistant to help brainstorm category gaps and refine the English translations.

Teamwork: Collaboration was the great way for validation of those riddles . So we worked independently , solve and evaluate the riddles without any bias.

Challenges: The most difficult part was translating poetic Bengali rhymes into English. It was challenging to maintain the rhythmic cadence and cultural essence without making the clue too obvious in English.

What I Enjoyed: I genuinely loved reconnecting with local folklore and seeing my teammates successfully deduce the answers based on our shared cultural background.

column19: We chose Economics and Food culture as wildcards because the fixed categories didn't have a clean home for the parts of Egyptian life where money, inflation, and daily consumption are inseparable from culture itself. A riddle like "a carton that became a symbol of rising prices" (red eggs) only makes sense if you understand that in Egypt, the price of eggs is a political event, not just a grocery item. Same for "open a new notebook", it's an economic phrase, but it's also a piece of neighborhood ritual between grocer and customer. These felt worth testing because they're exactly the kind of cultural-economic shorthand a model might surface-translate without actually understanding.
column22:
I wrote 25 riddles across 7 topics, leaning heavier on History (10) and Politics (4) because Egyptian history is so densely layered that adjacent events get easily confused, ex:Orabi vs. Sadat, 1919 vs. 1952, the Cairo Fire and the Citadel Massacre all live near each other in a way only locals untangle.

Most ideas came from memory like Tahrir chants, my family's reaction every time Al Ahly loses, the grocer saying "open a new notebook" at the start of the month. For history riddles I wrote from memory first, then verified dates and names so the clues stayed tight without turning into trivia.

The hardest part was writing clues that are obvious to an Egyptian but hard for a model. "Ruled while wearing a pilot's suit" is instantly Mubarak to anyone here, but a model only trained on formal descriptions has no chance. The 6th of October riddle took three drafts to land the bridge / metro station / square clue without leaking the year.

What I enjoyed most were the riddles that felt like documenting something rather than generating test data like Bread, Freedom, Human Dignity, the red-eggs carton, the Denshawai pigeon. Those carry real cultural weight.

If I did it again, I'd coordinate earlier with Nadine and Rawan to avoid overlap on the obvious history items, and keep a running notes file during the week, the best ideas came when I wasn't sitting down to write. "Open a new notebook" came to me while I was actually buying groceries.

column5: We translated the riddles using Google Translate, then manually verified and amended the translations. Overall, the machine translation quality was good enough, very few content or grammatical errors had to be corrected. Some of the grammatical nuance was lost in English, where most non-people, including geographic objects, animals, and plants, are denoted by "it", while the Belarusian version uses ён 'he', яна 'she', яно 'it', and even яны 'they' (in pluralia tantum nouns, see question 26). Some ambiguity was added inadvertently, as e.g. in question 66: Зялёны аматар мультфільмаў... -> A green cartoon lover..., where the intended reading 'green [cartoon lover]' is no longer unique. Transliterating proper names into English was a major issue in the reference answers; as a matter of practical convenience, we followed the English Wikipedia spellings, although some of them are in fact transliterated from Russian (question 7: Лідзія Ярмошына -> Lidia Yermoshina; question 25: Віцебск -> Vitebsk, etc.). Also, English translations of the riddles based on famous literary quotes don't seem to make much sense, even though they are accurate (see questions 31, 32, 61).

Then I asked the model, especially Gemini Flash version in my case. See if it can answer or not. If yes, I will change the word, phrase and the tone until I can trick it answering falsely. 

Next, I will try to look at the false answers, to see if my questions were actually confusing or the model did not have the knowledge and the link for the right answer.

column5:
Yes, definitely. Persian language has a long tradition of poetry, wordplay, and metaphor, and these are also very common in riddles. That made some of the riddles quite difficult to translate into English, especially with machine translation. In some cases, the machine gave me a rough option that still needed human correction. In other cases, it was almost no help at all.



1. The Iran riddle (with some modification!)



**Persian:**

«گربه‌سانی‌ام با سی‌ویک خال بر تن، هر خالم جهانی‌ست رنگارنگ.»



**English:**

“I am catlike, with thirty-one spots upon my body; each spot is a colorful world of its own.”



The answer is Iran. The map of Iran culturally is often compared to the shape of a cat, and the thirty-one spots refer to its thirty-one provinces.

The first automatic translation suggested “feline,” but that sounded like the subject was literally an animal from the cat family. I changed it to “catlike” because the clue is about the shape of Iran’s map. So the machine gave me a possible translation, but I still had to step in and choose the word that made sense culturally and preserved the metaphor.



2. The “من‌-شور” riddle



**Persian:**

«من‌-شور سنتی ایرانیم که در خلای خانه‌های قدیمی یافت می‌شوم.»



**Approximate English explanation:**

“I am a traditional Iranian object used for washing oneself, found in the washrooms of old houses.”


This one was much more difficult because it depends on Persian wordplay. The expression «من‌-شور» can be read as «من», meaning “me” or “self,” and «شور», which refers to washing. Together, they create the idea of something used to wash yourself.


The riddle also uses the word «خلا», which is an older Persian term for a toilet or washroom in traditional houses. (The word is still common in our culture!)


There is no simple English equivalent that keeps both the wordplay and the historical meaning. The machine could translate some of the words separately, but it could not understand how they worked together as a riddle. In this case, I had to interpret and rewrite the meaning myself.

It was a mix of reasons. We suggested cinema and food because they are popular topics and relatively easy to create riddles around.

I would have loved to include more language-based structures and dialects in the wild-card category. For example, Zargari is a secret form of Persian that people switch to when they want to speak without others understanding them. It is quite well known in Iran, and most people are at least familiar with the concept.

There are also other popular regional dialects, language games, and culturally specific forms of speech that could have made the riddles more unique. However, because they would have been more difficult to design and translate, there was not much interest in including them.
column22:
-I came up with most of my ideas through memory, personal experience, and observation. As an anthropologist, I pay close attention to everyday behavior, shared values, humor, concerns, and the topics that come up when Iranian families and communities gather. I also revisited a few popular films and songs to refresh my memory and identify cultural references and keywords that feel familiar to Iranian audiences but may not be obvious to people from other backgrounds.

-Our team divided the work by category, with each person taking two themes. I chose politics and everyday life because I felt they offered more room for cultural depth, metaphor, and humor. Some categories, such as history, national heritage, and geography, were more difficult because they could easily become factual rather than culturally expressive or metaphorical.

-Working with the team was both interesting and challenging. We sometimes had different ideas about what a riddle should look like. Some teammates preferred simple and direct language, while I was more interested in using the poetic structures and wordplay that are common in Persian riddles. At times, I felt some pressure to make my riddles follow the same language structure as the others. There were also differences in workload and level of commitment, which meant that some of us had to write additional riddles toward the end.

-What I enjoyed most was seeing the range of cultural references and perspectives that different people brought to the project. Super interesting!

-Next time, I would clarify the expectations earlier, particularly how creative, poetic, or culturally detailed the riddles could be, as well as how the workload would be divided.
